questions.title: Why can attention link distant words in a single step?
questions.hook: An RNN passes a signal through n steps to connect the first and last word, while self-attention connects every pair at once, trading sequential depth for n² work.
questions.quote: As noted in Table 1, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires O(n) sequential operations.

questions.title: How does a query pick which values to read?
questions.hook: Attention is a soft dictionary lookup: every key gets a score against the query, and the output blends all values by those scores rather than fetching just one.
questions.quote: An attention function can be described as mapping a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output, where the query, keys, values, and output are all vectors.

questions.title: Why divide the dot products by √dₖ?
questions.hook: Without the scale factor, dot-product variance grows with dₖ, so softmax saturates to near one-hot and its gradients almost vanish.
questions.quote: We suspect that for large values of dk, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients

questions.title: Why use 8 small heads instead of one big one?
questions.hook: One head has to average everything into a single blend, while eight 64-dim heads at the same total cost can each track a different relation, such as syntax or anaphora.
questions.quote: Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions. With a single attention head, averaging inhibits this.

questions.title: How does masking stop the decoder from cheating?
questions.hook: A triangle of −∞ entries in the score matrix, together with shifting the outputs right by one, lets the model train on all positions in parallel without ever seeing the future.
questions.quote: This masking, combined with fact that the output embeddings are offset by one position, ensures that the predictions for position i can depend only on the known outputs at positions less than i.

questions.title: How do sine waves tell the model word order?
questions.hook: Attention by itself ignores word order, so each position gets a fingerprint of sinusoids at geometrically spaced frequencies; any fixed offset is then a linear function of that fingerprint.
questions.quote: where pos is the position and i is the dimension. That is, each dimension of the positional encoding corresponds to a sinusoid.

q1.title: One hop vs. n hops: why attention reaches far words
q1.caption: A recurrent layer relays a signal through O(n) sequential steps to join the first and last word. A self-attention layer scores every pair at once, so the path is O(1), at the cost of O(n²·d) work per layer (Table 1, pp. 6–7).
q1.tryHint: Try: drag the sequence length up to 16 and press Replay. The attention signal arrives in 1 step while the RNN is still relaying.
q1.html:
Very long inputs? Restricted attention
Layer typeWork / layerSequential opsMax path
RecurrentO(n·d²)O(n)O(n)
Self-attentionO(n²·d)O(1)O(1)
From Table 1 (p. 6). Self-attention is cheaper per layer when n is smaller than d, the usual case for sentences (p. 7). The base model uses d_model = 512 (p. 3). The circles stand for words; the sequence length is illustrative.

explorables.label: Recurrent chain
explorables.blurb: An RNN computes each hidden state from the previous one, so a signal from the first word must pass through every position in order. That is O(n) sequential operations, and it cannot be parallelized within a sentence.
explorables.quote: This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, as memory constraints limit batching across examples.

explorables.label: Constant path length
explorables.blurb: In self-attention every position looks directly at every other position, so any two words are one step apart. The authors argue that shorter paths make long-range dependencies easier to learn.
explorables.quote: The shorter these paths between any combination of positions in the input and output sequences, the easier it is to learn long-range dependencies

explorables.label: The n² price
explorables.blurb: Connecting all pairs means computing n² query–key scores, for O(n²·d) work per layer. That is still cheaper than a recurrent layer's O(n·d²) whenever the sentence length n is below the model width d.
explorables.quote: In terms of computational complexity, self-attention layers are faster than recurrent layers when the sequence length n is smaller than the representation dimensionality d

explorables.label: Restricted attention
explorables.blurb: For very long inputs, each position could attend only to a local window of size r. This cuts the cost, but distant words are no longer one hop apart: the path grows to O(n/r).
explorables.quote: self-attention could be restricted to considering only a neighborhood of size r in the input sequence centered around the respective output position. This would increase the maximum path length to O(n/r).

q4.title: One blended head vs. eight specialised heads
q4.caption: The Transformer splits attention into h = 8 heads of 64 dims each, the same total cost as one 512-dim head, because a single head has to average (p. 5). Table 3 (A) reports single-head attention 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, and quality also drops with too many heads (p. 9). Fig. 4 shows sharp heads that resolve ‘its’ (p. 14).
q4.tryHint: Try: drag the heads slider from 1 to 8, then hover a column to see what that head tracks.
q4.html:
8
Hover or tap a column to see what that head tracks.

Cell shading and head roles are illustrative (toy weights for one query word). Total width is fixed at dmodel = 512, so dk = 512/h. BLEU/PPL are Table 3 rows (A), EN-DE dev set (p. 9).

explorables.label: Why one head blurs
explorables.blurb: One attention head yields a single weighted average over positions, so different relations get blended together. Separate heads can each focus on their own subspace and position.
explorables.quote: Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions. With a single attention head, averaging inhibits this.

explorables.label: Same cost, split 8 ways
explorables.blurb: Each of the 8 heads works in 64 dimensions, so together they span the same 512 as one full head. The total compute stays about the same.
explorables.quote: For each of these we use dk = dv = dmodel/h = 64. Due to the reduced dimension of each head, the total computational cost is similar to that of single-head attention with full dimensionality.

explorables.label: Heads vs. BLEU (Table 3)
explorables.blurb: Holding compute fixed, the paper varied h from 1 to 32. One head scored 24.9 dev BLEU, 8 and 16 heads scored 25.8, and 32 heads fell to 25.4.
explorables.quote: While single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, quality also drops off with too many heads.

explorables.label: Heads that resolve ‘its’
explorables.blurb: In layer 5, two heads attend very sharply from ‘its’ to ‘Law’ and ‘application’. This is a real example of individual heads specialising in a relation.
explorables.quote: Two attention heads, also in layer 5 of 6, apparently involved in anaphora resolution. Top: Full attentions for head 5. Bottom: Isolated attentions from just the word ‘its’ for attention heads 5 and 6.

q3.title: Why attention scores are divided by √dₖ
q3.caption: If q and k have unit-variance components, q·k has variance dₖ (p. 4, footnote 4). Large scores push softmax toward one-hot with tiny gradients, so Eq. 1 divides by √dₖ (p. 4).
q3.tryHint: Try: turn scaling off, drag dₖ up to 512, and watch the weights collapse onto one key as the gradient bar shrinks.
q3.html: paper uses dₖ = 64

explorables.label: Variance grows with dₖ
explorables.blurb: If query and key components are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product sums dₖ such terms. So its variance is dₖ, and scores spread out as √dₖ.
explorables.quote: To illustrate why the dot products get large, assume that the components of q and k are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1.

explorables.label: The 1/√dₖ scale
explorables.blurb: Dividing every score by √dₖ brings the spread back to about 1, whatever the key dimension. This single scaling factor is the only difference from plain dot-product attention.
explorables.quote: We compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by √dk, and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values.

explorables.label: Softmax weights
explorables.blurb: Softmax turns scores into weights that sum to 1. When the scores are far apart, almost all of the weight lands on a single key.
explorables.quote: The output is computed as a weighted sum of the values, where the weight assigned to each value is computed by a compatibility function of the query with the corresponding key.

explorables.label: Vanishing gradients
explorables.blurb: A nearly one-hot softmax has an almost flat derivative, so very little learning signal flows back through the scores. The paper suspects this is why unscaled dot products do worse at large dₖ.
explorables.quote: We suspect that for large values of dk, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients

explorables.label: dₖ = 64 per head
explorables.blurb: The base model splits d_model = 512 across 8 heads, so each head uses 64-dimensional keys. Without scaling, raw scores would have a standard deviation of about 8.
explorables.quote: In this work we employ h = 8 parallel attention layers, or heads. For each of these we use dk = dv = dmodel/h = 64.

q5.title: The causal mask: why the decoder can't peek ahead
q5.caption: In the decoder's self-attention, scores for later positions are set to −∞ before the softmax, so their weights become 0 (p. 5). Because the outputs are also shifted right by one, the prediction for position i can use only outputs before i (p. 3).
q5.tryHint: Try: switch the mask off, then slide the query row to see which answer token each row could copy.
q5.html:
3
Toy sentence, scores and weights are illustrative. The paper applies this mask inside every decoder self-attention layer.

explorables.label: The −∞ mask
explorables.blurb: Each score for a later position is replaced by −∞ before the softmax. Those entries then get exactly zero weight, so no information flows backward from the future.
explorables.quote: We implement this inside of scaled dot-product attention by masking out (setting to −∞) all values in the input of the softmax which correspond to illegal connections.

explorables.label: Outputs shifted right
explorables.blurb: The decoder's inputs are the target outputs moved one position later. Position i therefore reads the previous token, and together with the mask it can only use outputs before i.
explorables.quote: This masking, combined with fact that the output embeddings are offset by one position, ensures that the predictions for position i can depend only on the known outputs at positions less than i.

explorables.label: Auto-regressive output
explorables.blurb: At inference the decoder produces one token at a time. The mask makes training match this: every position is trained in parallel, yet each one sees only what would already have been generated.
explorables.quote: We need to prevent leftward information flow in the decoder to preserve the auto-regressive property.

explorables.label: Softmax attention weights
explorables.blurb: Each row of the matrix is a query's scaled dot products with all keys, passed through a softmax. The mask acts on these scores before the softmax runs.
explorables.quote: We compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by √dk, and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values.

q6.title: Sine waves as a position fingerprint
q6.caption: Each position gets a vector of sines and cosines whose wavelengths grow geometrically from 2π to 10000·2π; it is added to the word embedding so attention can see order (p. 6). Shifting by k rotates every (sin, cos) pair by a fixed angle, so PE(pos+k) is a linear function of PE(pos) (p. 6).
q6.tryHint: Try: drag the position slider to watch the fingerprint change, then vary the offset k and see each pair rotate by the same angle wherever pos is.
q6.html: ● pos   ○ pos + k

explorables.label: The sinusoid formula
explorables.blurb: Even dimensions get sin(pos/10000^(2i/d_model)) and odd dimensions get the matching cosine, so every dimension is a wave over positions. No parameters are learned.
explorables.quote: where pos is the position and i is the dimension. That is, each dimension of the positional encoding corresponds to a sinusoid.

explorables.label: Geometric wavelengths
explorables.blurb: Low dimensions oscillate fast (wavelength 2π) and high dimensions slowly (up to 10000·2π), each step multiplying the wavelength by a constant. Fast waves resolve neighbours; slow waves tell far positions apart.
explorables.quote: That is, each dimension of the positional encoding corresponds to a sinusoid. The wavelengths form a geometric progression from 2π to 10000 · 2π.

explorables.label: Position fingerprint
explorables.blurb: Attention alone has no notion of order, so each position's 512-number encoding is added to its token embedding (same d_model) at the bottom of the encoder and decoder stacks.
explorables.quote: Since our model contains no recurrence and no convolution, in order for the model to make use of the order of the sequence, we must inject some information about the relative or absolute position of the tokens in the sequence.

explorables.label: Offset as rotation
explorables.blurb: For each sin/cos pair, moving from pos to pos+k is a rotation by k·ω that does not depend on pos. That is why the authors expected the model could easily learn to attend by relative position.
explorables.quote: We chose this function because we hypothesized it would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset k, PEpos+k can be represented as a linear function of PEpos.

explorables.label: Learned vs. sinusoid
explorables.blurb: Swapping in learned position embeddings gave nearly the same result (25.7 vs 25.8 dev BLEU). The authors kept sinusoids because they may extrapolate to sequences longer than those seen in training.
explorables.quote: We also experimented with using learned positional embeddings [9] instead, and found that the two versions produced nearly identical results (see Table 3 row (E)).

q2.title: How a query picks which values to read
q2.caption: Each key is scored against the query by a dot product, scaled by 1/√dk, and softmaxed into weights; the output is a weighted sum of all values, not a single lookup (pp. 3–4). Multi-head attention repeats this in h = 8 parallel heads (p. 5).
q2.tryHint: Try: drag the query slider from “cat” to “mat” and watch the weights, and the blended output, shift. Then switch scaling off.

explorables.label: Dot-product score
explorables.blurb: Each key is compared with the query by a dot product: similar vectors give a high score. It is cheap because it is just matrix multiplication.
explorables.quote: While the two are similar in theoretical complexity, dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice, since it can be implemented using highly optimized matrix multiplication code.

explorables.label: Scaling by 1/√dk
explorables.blurb: Dot products grow with the key dimension, which would push softmax toward a near one-hot output with tiny gradients. Dividing by √dk keeps the scores in a gentler range.
explorables.quote: We suspect that for large values of dk, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients

explorables.label: Softmax weights
explorables.blurb: Softmax turns the scaled scores into positive weights that sum to 1. Every value gets some weight, so the lookup is soft rather than a single fetch.
explorables.quote: We compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by √dk, and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values.

explorables.label: Weighted sum of values
explorables.blurb: The output is every value vector multiplied by its weight and added up. Values whose keys match the query best dominate the blend.
explorables.quote: The output is computed as a weighted sum of the values, where the weight assigned to each value is computed by a compatibility function of the query with the corresponding key.

explorables.label: Multi-head attention
explorables.blurb: The paper runs this lookup 8 times in parallel on different learned projections (dk = dv = 64), so different heads can attend to different things before being concatenated.
explorables.quote: Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions. With a single attention head, averaging inhibits this.

q2/scaling-factor.title: Why attention divides scores by √dk
q2/scaling-factor.caption: Scaled dot-product attention divides the scores QKᵀ by √dk before the softmax (p. 4). If q and k have unit-variance components, q·k has variance dk, so large dk saturates the softmax into regions with tiny gradients (p. 4, footnote 4).
q2/scaling-factor.tryHint: Try: drag dk up to 512 with scaling off, then tick “Divide scores by √dk” and watch the weights spread back out.

explorables.label: Variance grows with dk
explorables.blurb: If each component of q and k has mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product sums dk such terms, so its variance is dk and its spread is √dk. Dividing by √dk brings the spread back to about 1.
explorables.quote: To illustrate why the dot products get large, assume that the components of q and k are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1.

explorables.label: Saturated softmax
explorables.blurb: When one score is far larger than the rest, softmax outputs nearly one-hot weights, and small changes to the scores barely change the output, so gradients become extremely small.
explorables.quote: We suspect that for large values of dk, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients

explorables.label: vs. additive attention
explorables.blurb: Additive attention scores keys with a small feed-forward network. It matches unscaled dot-product attention at small dk but beats it at large dk, which motivated the scaling factor.
explorables.quote: While for small values of dk the two mechanisms perform similarly, additive attention outperforms dot product attention without scaling for larger values of dk

explorables.label: Base model: dk = 64
explorables.blurb: With 8 heads and dmodel = 512, each head uses dk = 64, so scores are divided by √64 = 8 before the softmax.
explorables.quote: In this work we employ h = 8 parallel attention layers, or heads. For each of these we use dk = dv = dmodel/h = 64.

q1/constant-path.title: Constant path length: 1 hop vs. many
q1/constant-path.caption: Table 1 (p. 6) lists the maximum path length between any two positions for each layer type: O(1) for self-attention, O(n) for recurrent layers, O(log_k(n)) for dilated convolutions and O(n/r) for restricted self-attention. The paper argues that shorter paths make long-range dependencies easier to learn (p. 6).
q1/constant-path.tryHint: Try: drag the n slider to 16, then switch between Recurrent and Self-attention and watch the hop count.
q1/constant-path.html:
1hop from word 1 to word n
O(1)
O(n)
O(logk n)
O(n/r)
The catch: a single hop averages many attention-weighted positions, which blurs resolution; the paper counters this with multi-head attention (p. 2).

Big-O labels are from Table 1 (p. 6). Hop counts are illustrative toy counts for one path from word 1 to word n; *k = 2 and r = 5 are illustrative choices, not values from the paper.

explorables.label: O(1) path length
explorables.blurb: A self-attention layer links every position to every other in one step, so word 1 and word n are always one hop apart, whatever the sentence length.
explorables.quote: As noted in Table 1, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires O(n) sequential operations.

explorables.label: Recurrent O(n) chain
explorables.blurb: An RNN passes information one hidden state at a time, so the path between distant words grows with sequence length. The same sequential dependence also prevents parallelism within a training example.
explorables.quote: This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, as memory constraints limit batching across examples.

explorables.label: Convolution stacks
explorables.blurb: One convolution layer only sees a local window. Connecting every pair of positions takes O(n/k) stacked layers with contiguous kernels, or O(log_k(n)) with dilated ones.
explorables.quote: A single convolutional layer with kernel width k < n does not connect all pairs of input and output positions. Doing so requires a stack of O(n/k) convolutional layers in the case of contiguous kernels

explorables.label: Restricted attention
explorables.blurb: Limiting attention to a neighbourhood of size r would make very long sequences cheaper to process. The trade-off is that the maximum path length rises to O(n/r).
explorables.quote: self-attention could be restricted to considering only a neighborhood of size r in the input sequence centered around the respective output position. This would increase the maximum path length to O(n/r).

explorables.label: Cost: blurred focus
explorables.blurb: A constant path comes at a price: one attention step averages many weighted positions, which reduces effective resolution. Multi-head attention is the authors' fix for this.
explorables.quote: In the Transformer this is reduced to a constant number of operations, albeit at the cost of reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions, an effect we counteract with Multi-Head Attention

q3/scale-factor.title: The 1/√dₖ scale: keeping softmax out of saturation
q3/scale-factor.caption: Raw query–key dot products spread out like √dₖ, so the paper divides each one by √dₖ before the softmax (p. 4). Without the divide, large dₖ pushes the softmax toward a single winner with tiny gradients (p. 4). The model's heads use dₖ = 64 (p. 5).
q3/scale-factor.tryHint: Try: drag dₖ up to 512 with the divide switched off, then switch it back on and watch the weights relax.
q3/scale-factor.html: Illustrative: 8 keys with fixed toy values z, raw score = z·√dₖ (spread √dₖ, per the paper's footnote). 1−Σp² is an illustrative gradient-size measure.

explorables.label: Why spread is √dₖ
explorables.blurb: If query and key components are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product sums dₖ such terms. It has variance dₖ, so its typical size grows like √dₖ.
explorables.quote: To illustrate why the dot products get large, assume that the components of q and k are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1.

explorables.label: The ÷√dₖ step
explorables.blurb: Every query–key score is divided by √dₖ before the softmax. This one step is what the paper adds to plain dot-product attention.
explorables.quote: We compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by √dk, and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values.

explorables.label: Softmax saturation
explorables.blurb: When the inputs are widely spread, softmax puts almost all of the weight on one key. In that region its gradients become extremely small, which is the problem the scaling counteracts.
explorables.quote: We suspect that for large values of dk, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients

explorables.label: dₖ = 64 per head
explorables.blurb: The base model splits dmodel = 512 across 8 heads, so each head uses 64-dimensional keys. Without scaling, raw scores would spread about 8 times wider than unit spread.
explorables.quote: In this work we employ h = 8 parallel attention layers, or heads. For each of these we use dk = dv = dmodel/h = 64.

explorables.label: vs. additive attention
explorables.blurb: Prior work found that unscaled dot-product attention falls behind additive attention as dₖ grows. The 1/√dₖ factor keeps the faster dot-product form competitive.
explorables.quote: While for small values of dk the two mechanisms perform similarly, additive attention outperforms dot product attention without scaling for larger values of dk

q3/dot-variance.title: Why the dot product's spread grows as √dₖ
q3/dot-variance.caption: If query and key components are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, q·k is a sum of dₖ unit-variance terms, so its variance is dₖ (p. 4, footnote 4). The paper's heads use dₖ = 64 (p. 5) and rescale scores by 1/√dₖ to counteract this (p. 4).
q3/dot-variance.tryHint: Try: drag dₖ from 1 to 512 and watch the histogram widen, then tick “divide scores by √dₖ” to collapse it back.

explorables.label: Each term: mean 0, var 1
explorables.blurb: The paper's thought experiment treats every query and key component as an independent random number with mean 0 and variance 1, so each product qᵢkᵢ also has mean 0 and variance 1.
explorables.quote: To illustrate why the dot products get large, assume that the components of q and k are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1.

explorables.label: dₖ terms, variances add
explorables.blurb: Queries and keys have dimension dₖ, so the dot product adds up dₖ independent terms. Variances of independent terms add, giving a total variance of dₖ.
explorables.quote: The input consists of queries and keys of dimension dk, and values of dimension dv.

explorables.label: Spread = √dₖ
explorables.blurb: A variance of dₖ means a typical score sits about √dₖ from zero, so larger key dimensions give larger-magnitude scores. The paper notes that unscaled dot products fall behind additive attention at large dₖ.
explorables.quote: While for small values of dk the two mechanisms perform similarly, additive attention outperforms dot product attention without scaling for larger values of dk [3].

explorables.label: Dividing by √dₖ
explorables.blurb: Dividing each score by √dₖ divides its variance by dₖ, bringing it back to 1 no matter how wide the keys are. That division is the only thing separating the paper's attention from plain dot-product attention.
explorables.quote: We compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by √dk, and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values.

explorables.label: Saturated softmax
explorables.blurb: When scores spread widely, softmax puts almost all weight on a single key, and in that regime its gradients become extremely small. Scaling keeps scores in a range where learning can still proceed.
explorables.quote: We suspect that for large values of dk, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients

q1/recurrent-chain.title: The recurrent chain: one hidden state at a time
q1/recurrent-chain.caption: An RNN computes h_t from h_(t−1) and x_t, so the work runs in order along the sentence (p. 2). That means O(n) sequential operations and O(n) path length, compared with O(1) for self-attention (Table 1, p. 6).
q1/recurrent-chain.tryHint: Try: drag the sentence length slider and watch the step count, the hop count and the batch capacity change together.

explorables.label: Hidden state recurrence
explorables.blurb: Each hidden state h_t is computed from the previous state h_(t−1) and the current word. Position t cannot start until position t−1 has finished.
explorables.quote: Aligning the positions to steps in computation time, they generate a sequence of hidden states ht, as a function of the previous hidden state ht−1 and the input for position t.

explorables.label: O(n) sequential ops
explorables.blurb: A recurrent layer needs n steps that must run one after another. A self-attention layer connects all positions in a constant number of sequential steps.
explorables.quote: As noted in Table 1, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires O(n) sequential operations.

explorables.label: Path length O(n)
explorables.blurb: A signal from the first word travels through every intermediate state to reach the last one. The paper argues that shorter forward and backward paths make long-range dependencies easier to learn.
explorables.quote: The shorter these paths between any combination of positions in the input and output sequences, the easier it is to learn long-range dependencies [12].

explorables.label: Memory limits batching
explorables.blurb: Positions inside one sentence can't be computed in parallel, so speed has to come from batching many sentences at once. Longer sentences use more memory, which leaves room for fewer of them.
explorables.quote: This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, as memory constraints limit batching across examples.

explorables.label: Efficiency tricks
explorables.blurb: Factorization tricks and conditional computation made RNNs faster. The paper notes that the underlying sequential constraint remains.
explorables.quote: Recent work has achieved significant improvements in computational efficiency through factorization tricks [21] and conditional computation [32], while also improving model performance in case of the latter.

q2/compatibility-score.title: Dot-product score: how a query rates each key
q2/compatibility-score.caption: Each key's score is its dot product with the query, computed for all pairs at once as QKᵀ. Dividing by √dₖ stops scores from growing with dimension, so the softmax doesn't saturate into tiny gradients (p. 4).
q2/compatibility-score.tryHint: Try: turn scaling off, push dₖ up to 512, and watch the softmax snap onto a single key.
q2/compatibility-score.html:
QKᵀ: one matmulEvery query·key score computed at once.
÷ √dₖ scalingKeeps softmax out of its flat, tiny-gradient zone.
Variance grows with dₖRandom q·k has variance dₖ.
vs. additive attentionA small network instead of a dot product.

Vectors and score magnitudes are illustrative. dₖ = 64 is the paper's per-head key size (p. 5).

explorables.label: QKᵀ: one matmul
explorables.blurb: Queries are stacked into a matrix Q and keys into K, so a single matrix product QKᵀ yields every query–key score at once. That is why dot-product attention runs so fast on optimized hardware.
explorables.quote: In practice, we compute the attention function on a set of queries simultaneously, packed together into a matrix Q. The keys and values are also packed together into matrices K and V.

explorables.label: ÷ √dₖ scaling
explorables.blurb: Large dot products push the softmax toward a near one-hot output, where gradients almost vanish. Dividing every score by √dₖ keeps the scores in a range where the softmax can still learn.
explorables.quote: We suspect that for large values of dk, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients

explorables.label: Variance grows with dₖ
explorables.blurb: Suppose q and k have independent components with mean 0 and variance 1. Their dot product then sums dₖ terms, so it has variance dₖ and a typical size of √dₖ. Dividing by √dₖ cancels exactly that growth.
explorables.quote: To illustrate why the dot products get large, assume that the components of q and k are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1.

explorables.label: vs. additive attention
explorables.blurb: Additive attention scores a query–key pair with a one-hidden-layer network. The two methods have similar theoretical cost, but the dot product runs faster in practice. Additive attention wins at large dₖ only when the dot product is left unscaled.
explorables.quote: Additive attention computes the compatibility function using a feed-forward network with a single hidden layer. While the two are similar in theoretical complexity, dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice

q5/causal-mask.title: The −∞ mask: how softmax turns 'illegal' into zero
q5/causal-mask.caption: In decoder self-attention, every score for a key after the query is set to −∞ at the softmax input, inside scaled dot-product attention (p. 5; 'Mask (opt.)' in Fig. 2, p. 4). Because exp(−∞) = 0, those keys get exactly zero weight. Together with outputs shifted right by one, this means position i depends only on earlier outputs (p. 3).
q5/causal-mask.tryHint: Try: pick a query word, then switch the mask off and watch later words take attention weight.
q5/causal-mask.html: Query position:

explorables.label: Setting scores to −∞
explorables.blurb: The mask is applied inside scaled dot-product attention, just before the softmax. Every score that would let a position see a later one is replaced by −∞.
explorables.quote: We implement this inside of scaled dot-product attention by masking out (setting to −∞) all values in the input of the softmax which correspond to illegal connections.

explorables.label: Softmax → zero weight
explorables.blurb: Attention outputs are weighted sums of the values, and the softmax produces the weights. Since exp(−∞) is 0, a masked key contributes nothing. The remaining weights still sum to 1.
explorables.quote: The output is computed as a weighted sum of the values, where the weight assigned to each value is computed by a compatibility function of the query with the corresponding key.

explorables.label: Scaled dot-product scores
explorables.blurb: Before any masking, each query is dotted with every key and divided by √dk. These are the raw scores that the mask then edits.
explorables.quote: We compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by √dk, and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values.

explorables.label: Outputs shifted right
explorables.blurb: The mask works together with a one-position offset of the output embeddings. This combination makes the prediction at position i see only outputs before i.
explorables.quote: This masking, combined with fact that the output embeddings are offset by one position, ensures that the predictions for position i can depend only on the known outputs at positions less than i.

explorables.label: Auto-regressive property
explorables.blurb: At inference the decoder generates one symbol at a time, so during training it must not use future symbols. Blocking leftward information flow keeps training consistent with generation.
explorables.quote: Similarly, self-attention layers in the decoder allow each position in the decoder to attend to all positions in the decoder up to and including that position. We need to prevent leftward information flow in the decoder to preserve the auto-regressive property.

q4/single-head-averaging.title: Why one attention head blurs two relations
q4/single-head-averaging.caption: An attention head outputs a weighted sum of values (pp. 3–4). If one query needs two positions, one head can only average them, which the paper says inhibits attending to different subspaces at different positions. Separate learned projections let each head stay sharp (p. 5). The sentence and the sharp 'its' heads come from Fig. 4 (p. 14); the vectors are illustrative.
q4/single-head-averaging.tryHint: Try: drag the single head's mix slider to see that it can only trade 'Law' against 'application', then switch to 2 heads.

explorables.label: Output is an average
explorables.blurb: An attention head's output is a weighted sum of value vectors. If the weights split across two positions, the result falls between them and matches neither.
explorables.quote: The output is computed as a weighted sum of the values, where the weight assigned to each value is computed by a compatibility function of the query with the corresponding key.

explorables.label: Per-head subspaces
explorables.blurb: Each head first projects queries, keys and values with its own learned matrices. That gives each head a separate subspace in which it can attend to a different position.
explorables.quote: we found it beneficial to linearly project the queries, keys and values h times with different, learned linear projections to dk, dk and dv dimensions, respectively.

explorables.label: Concat, then project
explorables.blurb: The heads' outputs are placed side by side and projected again with W^O. Each head's sharp result reaches the next layer without being averaged into the others.
explorables.quote: These are concatenated and once again projected, resulting in the final values, as depicted in Figure 2.

explorables.label: Sharp heads for 'its'
explorables.blurb: In the paper's visualisation, two heads in layer 5 attend very sharply from 'its' to different words, 'Law' and 'application'. Each head does one job cleanly.
explorables.quote: Two attention heads, also in layer 5 of 6, apparently involved in anaphora resolution.

explorables.label: Cost of one head
explorables.blurb: In the ablation, compute was held constant while the number of heads changed. One head scored 0.9 BLEU below the best setting, and quality also fell with too many heads.
explorables.quote: While single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, quality also drops off with too many heads.

q5/shifted-right.title: Outputs shifted right: each position reads the past
q5/shifted-right.caption: The decoder's input is the target sentence moved one slot right, so position i receives the token from position i−1. Combined with the masked self-attention, the prediction at position i can only depend on outputs before i (p. 3, p. 5).
q5/shifted-right.tryHint: Try: turn off 'Shift right' or 'Causal mask' and slide the position to see exactly which future word leaks in.
q5/shifted-right.html: German tokens and the <s> start symbol are illustrative; the mechanism is from the paper (pp. 3, 5).

explorables.label: Shifted-right inputs
explorables.blurb: The decoder's input embeddings are the target outputs offset by one position, so the slot that predicts word i holds word i−1. Without the offset, each position would be handed the very word it is asked to predict.
explorables.quote: This masking, combined with fact that the output embeddings are offset by one position, ensures that the predictions for position i can depend only on the known outputs at positions less than i.

explorables.label: Causal mask
explorables.blurb: Inside scaled dot-product attention, scores for connections to later positions are set to −∞ before the softmax, so they get zero weight. The shift handles 'not myself'; the mask handles 'not the future'.
explorables.quote: We implement this inside of scaled dot-product attention by masking out (setting to −∞) all values in the input of the softmax which correspond to illegal connections.

explorables.label: Auto-regressive decoding
explorables.blurb: At generation time the decoder produces one symbol at a time and feeds it back as the next input. The shift plus mask make training match this: each position sees only what would already have been generated.
explorables.quote: Given z, the decoder then generates an output sequence (y1, ..., ym) of symbols one element at a time. At each step the model is auto-regressive [10], consuming the previously generated symbols as additional input when generating the next.

explorables.label: Next-token softmax
explorables.blurb: Each decoder position's output goes through a learned linear layer and a softmax to give probabilities for the next token. Because inputs are shifted, position i's output is scored against target word i.
explorables.quote: We also use the usual learned linear transformation and softmax function to convert the decoder output to predicted next-token probabilities.

q4/same-cost-split.title: Same cost, split 8 ways: 8 × 64 = 512
q4/same-cost-split.caption: With h = 8 heads of dk = dv = 64 each, the heads together span dmodel = 512, so the total cost is similar to one full-width head (p. 5). Table 3 rows (A) vary h while keeping computation constant (p. 9).
q4/same-cost-split.tryHint: Try: switch h between 1 and 32. Each head gets narrower, but the total width, the weight count and the compute bar stay the same, while BLEU changes.
q4/same-cost-split.html: Heads h (Table 3 A):

explorables.label: dk = dv = 512/h = 64
explorables.blurb: Each head works in a smaller space: the model width 512 is divided by the number of heads, so with 8 heads each query, key and value is 64-dimensional.
explorables.quote: In this work we employ h = 8 parallel attention layers, or heads. For each of these we use dk = dv = dmodel/h = 64.

explorables.label: Per-head projections
explorables.blurb: Every head has its own learned matrices that map the 512-dim queries, keys and values down to dk, dk and dv. Eight 512×64 matrices hold as many weights as one 512×512 matrix.
explorables.quote: we found it beneficial to linearly project the queries, keys and values h times with different, learned linear projections to dk, dk and dv dimensions, respectively.

explorables.label: Concat + Wᴼ
explorables.blurb: The h head outputs of size dv are stacked back into one h·dv = 512 vector, then projected by Wᴼ, so the sub-layer's output keeps the same shape as a single full head's.
explorables.quote: These are concatenated and once again projected, resulting in the final values, as depicted in Figure 2.

explorables.label: Table 3 (A): vary h
explorables.blurb: The authors swept h = 1, 4, 8, 16, 32 and adjusted dk and dv to keep compute constant. Quality peaks at 8 to 16 heads (25.8 dev BLEU) and drops at both extremes.
explorables.quote: In Table 3 rows (A), we vary the number of attention heads and the attention key and value dimensions, keeping the amount of computation constant, as described in Section 3.2.2.

explorables.label: Why not one head?
explorables.blurb: A single head has to blend everything into one weighted average. At equal cost it scored 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, although quality also drops with too many heads.
explorables.quote: Multi-head attention allows the model to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions. With a single attention head, averaging inhibits this.

q6/sinusoid-formula.title: Inside the sinusoid formula: one frequency per pair
q6/sinusoid-formula.caption: Each dimension pair (2i, 2i+1) of the positional encoding is a sine and cosine of pos, where d_model = 512 (p. 3). The wavelengths form a geometric progression from 2π to 10000·2π, and PE(pos+k) is a linear function of PE(pos) (p. 6).
q6/sinusoid-formula.tryHint: Try: drag the dimension-pair slider from 0 toward 255 and watch the wave stretch as the marker slides along the wavelength bar.
q6/sinusoid-formula.html:
PE(pos, 2i) = sin( pos / 100002i/dmodel )
PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos( pos / 100002i/dmodel )
dmodel = 512, so i runs 0…255 (256 sin/cos pairs). Nothing here is learned. Positions 0–64 and the rotation picture are our illustration. vs. learned embeddings

explorables.label: The sin/cos pair
explorables.blurb: Dimension 2i gets a sine and dimension 2i+1 the cosine of the same frequency, so each pair traces a point around a circle as pos grows. Every pair has its own speed.
explorables.quote: There are many choices of positional encodings, learned and fixed [9]. In this work, we use sine and cosine functions of different frequencies

explorables.label: Offsets are linear
explorables.blurb: The authors chose sinusoids because shifting by a fixed offset k turns PE(pos) into PE(pos+k) through a linear map. For a sin/cos pair that map is a rotation that does not depend on pos.
explorables.quote: we hypothesized it would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset k, PEpos+k can be represented as a linear function of PEpos.

explorables.label: Geometric wavelengths
explorables.blurb: Because i appears in the exponent of 10000, wavelength grows geometrically with i. Low pairs cycle every ~6 positions, and the highest pairs barely move over a sentence.
explorables.quote: That is, each dimension of the positional encoding corresponds to a sinusoid. The wavelengths form a geometric progression from 2π to 10000 · 2π.

explorables.label: Vs. learned embeddings
explorables.blurb: Learned positional embeddings gave nearly identical results (25.7 vs 25.8 dev BLEU, Table 3 row E). The fixed sinusoids were kept because they might extrapolate to longer sequences.
explorables.quote: We chose the sinusoidal version because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training.

q6/geometric-wavelengths.title: Geometric wavelengths: from 2π to 10000·2π
q6/geometric-wavelengths.caption: Each positional-encoding dimension is a sinusoid, and the wavelengths form a geometric progression from 2π to 10000·2π (p. 6). This diagram shows six evenly spaced pairs out of 256, for d_model = 512 (p. 3). Fast rows separate neighbouring positions, while slow rows keep changing smoothly over long spans.
q6/geometric-wavelengths.tryHint: Try: set the offset k to 1, then to 80, and compare how far the dots move on the fast row versus the slow row.
q6/geometric-wavelengths.html:
Each row is a wave at one dimension
The x-axis is the token position (0–200). Each row repeats every λ positions, and λ grows by the same factor from row to row.
sin + cos at each frequencyeven dims use sin, odd dims use cos
PE(pos+k) is linear in PE(pos)why the ghost is reachable from pos
Only 6 of 256 pairs are drawn (i = 0, 51, …, 255). λ = 2π·10000^(2i/512).

explorables.label: Fastest wave (λ = 2π)
explorables.blurb: Dimension pair i = 0 repeats roughly every 6.3 positions. It separates neighbouring tokens sharply, but on its own it would confuse positions that are a full cycle apart.
explorables.quote: where pos is the position and i is the dimension. That is, each dimension of the positional encoding corresponds to a sinusoid.

explorables.label: Slowest wave (≈10000·2π)
explorables.blurb: The last pair has a wavelength near 10000·2π, so it barely moves across a sentence. It changes smoothly and never wraps around at ordinary lengths. The authors hoped a smooth encoding like this might carry over to sequences longer than those seen in training.
explorables.quote: We chose the sinusoidal version because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training.

explorables.label: Geometric progression
explorables.blurb: Each step in i multiplies the wavelength by the same factor, 10000^(2/512) ≈ 1.037. That is why the 256 wavelengths sit evenly spaced on a log scale between 2π and 10000·2π.
explorables.quote: That is, each dimension of the positional encoding corresponds to a sinusoid. The wavelengths form a geometric progression from 2π to 10000 · 2π.

explorables.label: Sine + cosine pairs
explorables.blurb: Each frequency is used twice: even dimensions take the sine and odd dimensions take the cosine. Together the pair acts like a point rotating around a circle at that frequency.
explorables.quote: In this work, we use sine and cosine functions of different frequencies:

explorables.label: Offset k is linear
explorables.blurb: Because each frequency has a sin/cos pair, shifting by a fixed k rotates every pair by a fixed angle. That makes PE(pos+k) a linear function of PE(pos), which the authors hypothesized would help attention by relative position.
explorables.quote: we hypothesized it would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset k, P Epos+k can be represented as a linear function of P Epos.
